name: Where the Streets Have No Name

podcast.body: When this song was released as a 12-inch vinyl single, U2 took the opportunity to include three additional tracks as bonus material on the B-side. This exemplified the trend of 12-inch singles offering more space for bonus tracks than traditional 7-inch releases. "When they issued where the streets have no name on a vinyl 12 inch single, they had no trouble finding solid material for the B side. Streets came with not one, not two, but three extra tracks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Digital Debris Part 1: B-Sides and Bonus Tracks

podcast.body: The Edge brought demos to the *Joshua Tree* sessions declaring he had written "the most amazing guitar part he'd ever written in his life" and did a little dance in his home studio. The band then spent enormous amounts of rehearsal time and recording tape unable to nail the song — the timing changes and chord changes proved too complex. Co-producer Brian Eno became so frustrated that he proposed erasing the tape and starting from scratch. Engineer Pat McCarthy disagreed and physically blocked access to the tape machine with his body, resulting in a physical confrontation. The band eventually built the song from three separate basic takes, making it a Frankenstein composite. Even then, Eno and co-producer Daniel Lanois found it too much; Steve Lillywhite was brought in to finish the track, to Eno's annoyance. The result opens the album. "There's the intro, the first two verses, and the third verse. This is a Frankenstein monster of a song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: The opening track from *The Joshua Tree*. It begins with a synthesizer arrangement that fades in from silence, changing chords for the first 40 seconds to create a cinematic effect reminiscent of a sunrise or sunset over a vast desert. At 40 seconds, The Edge introduces a chiming arpeggio in an unusual time signature, while the synth chords continue to build. The time signature then shifts at one minute and seven seconds as Adam and Larry join with the rhythm section, building energy for another 35 seconds before Bono starts singing at one minute and 46 seconds. This track is considered one of U2's best and one of the greatest songs of the 20th century, serving as a prime example of a song with a lengthy introduction that would struggle to find success in today's short-attention-span music consumption culture. "Track 1 opens with a synthesizer arrangement fedient from the silence. It changes chords several times over the first 40 seconds. It's very cinematic effect, conjuring visions of a sunrise or sunset over something like a vast desert."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: The opening track of "The Joshua Tree," known for its cinematic quality, beginning with a synthesizer pulse and evolving into an expansive sound described as having "a bit of sunrise." Originally titled "White City," Bono envisioned it as a utopian place free from judgment, racism, and poverty. The Edge initially struggled with a complex time signature change (from 6/8 to 4/4) in the intro, which Daniel Landwom helped resolve using a blackboard. Brian Eno, due to impatience, instructed a tape op to erase the track, but the op refused. "Well it has a bit of sunrise. And it does not, you know, as if the day is opening and it suggests that there's a doorway to a certain kind of dimension."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This famous song is directly inspired by the religious segregation prevalent in Belfast. The city of Belfast and its religious divisions have consistently been important political themes for U2, and in this period, the political-religious-spiritual content of their music became increasingly evident. "la famosa canción, buen de Suís Hathno Name, que realmente está inspirada en Belfast en la segregación religiosa que hay en la ciudad."

This opening track from *The Joshua Tree* is renowned for its cinematic and extensive introduction: it starts with a keyboard drone, an organ resolving at 25 seconds, The Edge's guitar fading in at 42 seconds, Adam Clayton's bass at 1:09, Larry Mullen Jr.'s drumming thereafter, a chord change at 1:41, and Bono's vocals finally entering at 1:46, forming a glorious start to a classic rock album. "It starts with where the streets have no name. The song is a brilliant opener to the album with a cinematic introduction evocative of a sunrise or sunset."
